title: The subject of the sentence and expressing desire
summary: Japanese happily lets things be the main carriage, so "I like coffee" is really "coffee is pleasing". The same logic explains ほしい, たい and たがる.

blocks.text: English wants a person, usually "I", to be the actor of every sentence. Japanese is happy to put a **thing** in the main carriage. This explains the sentences that confuse learners most.
"I like coffee" is not about I

blocks.jp: 私はコーヒーが好きだ。
blocks.en: As for me, coffee is pleasing. (I like coffee.)

blocks.text: The main carriage is コーヒー. 好き is a な-type word meaning "pleasing".

"I" is only the **topic**. The main carriage is **coffee**, and the engine says coffee is "pleasing". Textbooks that say が marks "the object" here teach you something that never happens: が always marks the main carriage.

blocks.en: The book is understandable. (I understand the book.)

blocks.text: Wanting: ほしい and たい
**ほしい** is an い-adjective meaning "is wanted". The thing wanted is the main carriage. The wish itself belongs to the speaker, so it is not written.

blocks.en: (I) want a kitten. (A kitten is wanted.)

blocks.text: To want to **do** something, attach the adjective **たい** to the **い-stem** of the verb: 食べる → 食べ**たい**. Again the thing is the main carriage: "crepes are eating-desired". With nothing else named, the zero is the speaker.

blocks.jp: 私はクレープが食べたい。

blocks.text: Feelings of other people: がる

Words like ほしい, たい and 怖い describe a feeling **from the inside**: the speaker's. They cannot describe someone else's feelings, because you cannot see them. For other people, attach **がる** ("shows signs of") to the stem. がる makes a verb, because all you can see is behavior.

blocks.en: Ghosts are scary. (I am scared of ghosts.)

blocks.jp: さくらがケーキを欲しがる。
blocks.en: Sakura wants cake. (she shows signs of wanting it)

items: **が** marks the main carriage even in **好きだ**, **ほしい**, **たい** and **わかる**.
**ほしい**: "is wanted" (い-adjective). **い-stem + たい**: "is desired to do".
Feelings from the inside belong to the **speaker**; for someone else, add **がる**.
The topic (**私は**) is only the one who feels it.

questions.instruction: In 私はコーヒーが好きだ, which word is the main carriage?
questions.note: コーヒーが is the main carriage; 私は is only the topic.
が marks the main carriage, even here.
That is why the thing wanted takes が.

questions.instruction: Which says "I want to eat crepes"?
options: 私はクレープが食べたい
私はクレープを食べるたい
私はクレープが食べるたい
私はクレープが食べない
questions.note: 食べ + たい, on the い-stem.
A hidden main carriage defaults to the speaker.

questions.instruction: Which describes someone else wanting cake?
options: さくらがケーキを欲しがる
さくらがケーキがほしい
さくらはケーキがほしい
さくらがケーキをほしいる
questions.note: For another person, use がる: she shows signs of wanting it.

questions.prompt: "I like coffee" mirrors the Japanese grammar exactly.
questions.note: Japanese says: as for me, coffee is pleasing.

questions.instruction: What does 本がわかる mean, literally?
questions.note: The book is the main carriage; わかる says it is understandable.

options: It shows signs of a feeling, for another person

questions.instruction: おばけが怖い。 Who is scared, and what is the cause?
options: The speaker (a zero) is scared; the ghost is the cause
questions.note: 怖い describes a feeling from the inside; the ghost is the main carriage.
